blogs.title: Time's Trouble: When Does Exemption 7(A) Lose Its Clamp?
blogs.description: This article examines how the D.C. Circuit’s ruling in Farahi confirms that the FOIA Exemption 7(A) hinges on whether an investigation is still pending or reasonably anticipated, even after several years of delay. It traces the pendency doctrine’s roots in CREW and Juarez, evaluates the court’s application to a protracted counterterrorism probe, and discusses what this means for future FOIA litigants facing long‑running investigations.

blogs.title: Ex Parte FOIA Declarations: Transparency vs. Security in the Farahi Case
blogs.description: The Farahi case spotlights the tightrope FOIA courts walk between public access and national‑security concerns. This post unpacks the court’s heavy reliance on sealed ex‑parte affidavits, the deference standards that apply to law‑enforcement agencies, and how the balance of secrecy and transparency has evolved in the post‑9/11 era.

blogs.title: Segregation Scruples: The ‘No Meaningful Segregable Portion’ Rule in FOIA
blogs.description: The court’s affirmation that a 10,750‑page, 80‑CD FBI file contained no reasonably segregable non‑exempt material sheds light on the practical limits of the ‘no meaningful segregable portion’ doctrine. This piece reviews precedents like Mead and Juarez, explains how the ‘reasonable steps’ requirement operates, and outlines strategies FOIA seekers might use when confronting sprawling records.

blogs.title: FOIA, Immigration, and Counterterrorism: A Cross‑Jurisdictional Legal Minefield
blogs.description: By intertwining removal proceedings, asylum claims, and counterterrorism investigations, the Farahi case exposes the intricate nexus between immigration law and FOIA disclosure. The post explores how FOIA requests are treated when an individual’s immigration status and alleged terrorist ties overlap, the statutory safeguards that govern such requests, and policy implications for safeguarding both national security and individual rights.
